This assertion appears in the SEC's characterization of the case against Bankman-Fried, who faces trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The argument positions the scale and direct nature of Bankman-Fried's personal appropriation of customer assets as the defining feature that transformed FTX from a failed business into a criminal enterprise, rather than attributing losses to mere operational mismanagement or market conditions.

# Bankman-Fried accused of spending billions in stolen FTX deposits on real estate, investments, and loan repayment

According to the indictment, Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" for three purposes: purchasing over $200 million in real estate for himself, making billions of dollars in personal investments, and repaying Alameda Research's lenders. The government also alleges he used more than $100 million of customer funds for political contributions, though those contributions are not part of the formal charges.

Prosecutor Thane Rehn stated that Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money—both cash and crypto—by using Caroline Ellison, Alameda's CEO, as a front. The prosecution contended that under this structure, Bankman-Fried directed FTX customer deposits into Alameda, a crypto hedge fund he also owned, while concealing the flow and forging financial documents to lenders and investors. The prosecution characterized Alameda Research as "the key to his alleged scheme" through which billions were allegedly stolen from thousands of victims.

The warrant for this claim was the gap between Bankman-Fried's public assurances that customer money was "safe and secure" and his alleged secret use of customer funds through Alameda Research to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky investments. TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games planned to argue Google maintains anticompetitive control over Android app distribution. qid: What company spends billions to maintain its default search engine status on various platforms, influences local search rankings with specific criteria, and is accused by news publishers of anticompetitive practices that harm their revenue, according to articles from The Verge and TechCrunch?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle argues Google 'starves the free press' through content redistribution costing publishers billions

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based news publisher, filed a class action antitrust lawsuit accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior. The complaint asserts that Google is "starving the free press" by redistributing publishers' content across its own products—including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI—while causing publishers to lose "billions of dollars" in revenue. The suit argues that Google extracts news publishers' content, readers, and advertising revenue through technologies ranging from the Knowledge Graph (launched 2012) to Featured Snippets, fundamentally diverting traffic and income away from news organizations.


---


# DOJ argues Google's defaults and data denial block search competition

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the U.S. Department of Justice contends Google uses "its platforms and deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thus hindering competitors from accessing the data they'd need to improve their products." The government's theory links Google's paid default arrangements—including the $26.3 billion Google spent in 2021 to be the default search engine across browsers, phones and platforms—to competitive harm. By securing default placement through deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla, the DOJ argues, Google monopolizes query data collection. This data access gap prevents rival search engines like Microsoft's Bing and DuckDuckGo from gathering sufficient user information to enhance their products enough to compete effectively. The lawsuit, filed in January by the Department of Justice and eight states including New York, California, and Colorado, seeks to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising."


---


# Default search engine placement as scarce asset in Google antitrust case

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google centers on deals making Google the default search engine across devices and browsers. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a device or browser maker, requiring no user setup action to deploy. This makes the placement itself—not the search quality—the scarce asset that distributors like Apple and Samsung sell to Google. The trial revealed Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to secure default status across platforms. Internal Google data showed that when users switched their browser homepage to Google, they conducted "15% more Google searches," demonstrating the value Google placed on default positioning independent of product superiority.


---


# Google's defense: default status earned through superior product, not illegal conduct

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google CEO Sundar Pichai defended the company's business model during antitrust testimony, arguing that paying $26.3 billion annually to partners like Apple for default search engine placement is lawful competitive practice. Pichai contended that "it's just doing business. Everybody wants Google as the default engine because it's the best." The company maintains that partners choose Google voluntarily because of superior quality and that consumers benefit from this arrangement, not that the expenditure itself constitutes anticompetitive conduct. Google frames its strategy as data collection for product improvement across devices, not market foreclosure. This argument directly counters the Department of Justice's claim that Google uses such deals to block competition and prevent rivals from accessing data needed to improve their offerings.


---


# Google's circular justification for default search payments via data acquisition

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in the U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's default search engine payments by advancing a reinforcing cycle: default placement generates more queries, which yields more data, which improves search quality, thereby justifying continued default spending. Pichai stated that Google "pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices." In 2021, Google spent $26.3 billion on default placements, including $18 billion to Apple. A 2007 internal Google email presented to Pichai showed that homepage changes to Google correlated with 15% more searches, while switching away reduced searches 27%. This model—that defaults drive query volume, query volume drives data quality, and quality justifies further payments—represents Google's testimony, not established economic fact.


---


# Google's 2021 default search spend and Chrome preinstall efforts

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-13 that Google spent "$26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms" and separately "tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones," according to disclosures in the U.S. Department of Justice's antitrust trial against the search giant. These revelations emerged from the Justice Department's landmark case arguing that Google uses exclusive deals with partners to block competition in search.


---


# Rival search engines claim default placement, not quality, limits market share

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and DuckDuckGo's CEO testified in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google that their search engines would have achieved competitive scale with Apple's default placement. Nadella stated he was willing to spend $15 billion annually to secure Bing as Apple's default search engine, suggesting that access to paid default placement—not product quality—determines rival search engine market share. This testimony proposes a testable counterfactual: a search engine with comparable product quality given equal access to default placement deals would reach competitive scale. The hypothesis is falsified if a rival offered such placement fails to grow market share substantially, or confirmed if placement correlates with competitor growth independent of product improvements.


---


# Complaint alleges SGE designed to retain users within Google while reusing publisher content

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action lawsuit filed by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle against Google and Alphabet contends that Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) is structured to discourage end-users from visiting news publishers' websites. The complaint argues that SGE "keeps users in Google's 'walled garden' as it 'plagiarizes' their content" while offering conversational search capabilities. According to the suit, this design operates as anticompetitive behavior harming the digital news publishing line of commerce. The complaint further notes that publishers cannot block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot, making opt-out impossible despite the technology's traffic-diverting effects.


---


# Kent Walker defends Google's default search status as merit-based, not anticompetitive

The Age reported on 2023-10-22 that Google's president of global affairs Kent Walker argued the company's dominance in search results from user preference rather than anticompetitive conduct. Walker claimed users, browsers and device makers favour Google Search "simply because it was the best in the business." He contended that default status is not determinative of market power, asserting that "people don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to." Walker pointed to user behaviour as evidence: when Mozilla made Yahoo the default on Firefox, most users switched back to Google; when setting up Windows devices, users frequently bypass Microsoft's default to search "Google" on Bing despite Microsoft making this "very annoying to do." He argued the lawsuit "simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today," suggesting easy switching between search providers undermines claims of lock-in effects.


---


# Apple received $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion default search payments in 2021

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, "about $18 billion of that total amount went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier this month." This represented Google's largest single payment among deals with companies including Samsung and Mozilla. Google has maintained its default search arrangement with Apple since 2003.


---


# DOJ's antitrust theory: Google's default-engine agreements create de facto search dominance across platforms

The Verge reported on 2023-09-26 that the US Department of Justice's case against Google centers on default search agreements as the mechanism of anticompetitive harm. During testimony by Apple executive Eddy Cue in US v. Google, DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw focused on the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Google and Apple, which has made Google the default search engine on Apple devices since 2002. The Justice Department's strategy targets "the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform." The DOJ alleges these default arrangements, rather than superior product quality, lock in Google's dominance across consumer entry points to search, foreclosing rivals' access.

The Verge reported on 2023-09-26 that the US Department of Justice's case against Google centers on default search agreements as the mechanism of anticompetitive harm. During testimony by Apple executive Eddy Cue in US v. Google, DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw focused on the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Google and Apple, which has made Google the default search engine on Apple devices since 2002. The Justice Department's strategy targets "the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform." The DOJ alleges these default arrangements, rather than superior product quality, lock in Google's dominance across consumer entry points to search, foreclosing rivals' access.


---


# Default search engine placement as scarce asset in Google antitrust case

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google centers on deals making Google the default search engine across devices and browsers. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a device or browser maker, requiring no user setup action to deploy. This makes the placement itself—not the search quality—the scarce asset that distributors like Apple and Samsung sell to Google. The trial revealed Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to secure default status across platforms. Internal Google data showed that when users switched their browser homepage to Google, they conducted "15% more Google searches," demonstrating the value Google placed on default positioning independent of product superiority.


---


# DOJ argues Google's defaults and data denial block search competition

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the U.S. Department of Justice contends Google uses "its platforms and deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thus hindering competitors from accessing the data they'd need to improve their products." The government's theory links Google's paid default arrangements—including the $26.3 billion Google spent in 2021 to be the default search engine across browsers, phones and platforms—to competitive harm. By securing default placement through deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla, the DOJ argues, Google monopolizes query data collection. This data access gap prevents rival search engines like Microsoft's Bing and DuckDuckGo from gathering sufficient user information to enhance their products enough to compete effectively. The lawsuit, filed in January by the Department of Justice and eight states including New York, California, and Colorado, seeks to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising."


---


# Google disputes Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit as meritless

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that Google rejected the antitrust lawsuit filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle. A Google spokesperson characterized the complaint as "meritless," pushing back against allegations that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior through its use of publishers' content and AI technologies like Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot to harm news publishers' revenues.


---


# Complaint alleges SGE designed to retain users within Google while reusing publisher content

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-15 that a class action lawsuit filed by Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle against Google and Alphabet contends that Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) is structured to discourage end-users from visiting news publishers' websites. The complaint argues that SGE "keeps users in Google's 'walled garden' as it 'plagiarizes' their content" while offering conversational search capabilities. According to the suit, this design operates as anticompetitive behavior harming the digital news publishing line of commerce. The complaint further notes that publishers cannot block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot, making opt-out impossible despite the technology's traffic-diverting effects.


---


# Google's defense: default status earned through superior product, not illegal conduct

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that Google CEO Sundar Pichai defended the company's business model during antitrust testimony, arguing that paying $26.3 billion annually to partners like Apple for default search engine placement is lawful competitive practice. Pichai contended that "it's just doing business. Everybody wants Google as the default engine because it's the best." The company maintains that partners choose Google voluntarily because of superior quality and that consumers benefit from this arrangement, not that the expenditure itself constitutes anticompetitive conduct. Google frames its strategy as data collection for product improvement across devices, not market foreclosure. This argument directly counters the Department of Justice's claim that Google uses such deals to block competition and prevent rivals from accessing data needed to improve their offerings.


---


# DOJ's January 2023 ad-tech case targets Google's digital advertising monopoly

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that a separate lawsuit filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice along with eight states—including New York, California, and Colorado—focuses on digital advertising rather than search. This ad-tech case aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising," distinct from the 2020 antitrust claim over Google's search dominance. The government has argued that Google uses its platforms and partner deals to block competition in both search and advertising, preventing competitors from accessing the data needed to improve their products.


---


# DOJ's theory of Google monopoly: platform defaults and exclusive deals starve rivals of query data

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-13 that the Justice Department's core antitrust argument against Google links the company's platform ownership and partner agreements to search monopoly power. The government has argued that "Google uses its platforms and deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thus hindering competitors from accessing the data they'd need to improve their products."

The theory posits a cycle: Google's default search placement across devices and exclusive distribution deals with manufacturers suppress rival search engines from acquiring users and queries. This query scarcity prevents competitors from collecting the behavioral data necessary to improve search quality and attract additional users. The DOJ cited that Google receives 16 times more daily data than Bing, underscoring rivals' data disadvantage. A ruling against Google could require sharing APIs with third-party developers and banning exclusive deals with smartphone makers and wireless carriers.


---


# The 2020 Google search dominance antitrust lawsuit, tried in October 2023

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that the antitrust trial underway in October 2023 concerns a "2020 antitrust claim over Google's dominance in the online search market," distinct from a separate January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states targeting Google's digital advertising practices. The search case addresses Google's default search engine agreements with partners like Apple, with CEO Sundar Pichai testifying to defend the company's business tactics. This lawsuit is separate from the advertising-focused antitrust claim filed later.


---


# US v Google verdict hypothesized to influence parallel Big Tech antitrust cases

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-13 that the outcome of the Department of Justice's antitrust case against Google could "have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases." The publication identified three parallel proceedings potentially affected: the FTC's September lawsuit against Amazon alleging anticompetitive strategies to maintain monopoly power; the DOJ's years-long investigation of Apple over third-party app policies; and the ongoing FTC case against Facebook seeking divestiture of Instagram and WhatsApp. This hypothesis is falsified if those cases proceed and settle without demonstrable influence from Judge Amit Mehta's ruling on Google's search and advertising practices.

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-31 that during the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw presented CEO Sundar Pichai with a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting. Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that defence lawyer Mark Cohen argued Sam Bankman-Fried acted in good faith as a startup founder. Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that Mark Cohen, lawyer for Sam Bankman-Fried, argued the defendant demonstrated his innocence through his actions as FTX collapsed. Cohen contended that "when the walls came closing in," Bankman-Fried "was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole," behavior inconsistent with guilt. Cohen concluded his opening statement by asserting that Bankman-Fried, who "started and built two billion-dollar businesses," ultimately "didn't steal any money."


---


# The Verge's October 31, 2023 index of Bankman-Fried's June 2022 testimony on the $8 billion accounting gap

The Verge reported on 2023-10-31 that Sam Bankman-Fried testified about his response to a major FTX accounting discrepancy in June 2022. The article structures around six key moments: (1) a software bug that initially showed Alameda owed FTX $8 billion; (2) Bankman-Fried's discovery of the fiat@ftx account tracking this debt, which he didn't understand until October; (3) his employees' remark that "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting"; (4) his admission under judicial pressure that Adam Yedidia had told him about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court; (5) his lack of any internal controls or policies preventing Alameda from spending FTX customer deposits; and (6) an Alameda balance sheet from June 13, 2022 labeled "ftx borrows" that Bankman-Fried testified he was "pretty hazy on." The article emphasizes the absence of investigative or disciplinary action despite the magnitude of the discrepancy.


---


# Prosecutor Rehn's central allegation: Bankman-Fried's success built entirely on concealed fraud

Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that prosecutor Thane Rehn framed Sam Bankman-Fried's rise as fundamentally fraudulent in his opening statement at trial. Rehn argued that "all of that, all of it, was built on lies" and "behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." The warrant for this claim was the gap between Bankman-Fried's public assurances that customer money was "safe and secure" and his alleged secret use of customer funds through Alameda Research to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky investments. Rehn characterized Bankman-Fried not as a startup "boy" but as a "man" who stole billions from thousands of victims.


---


# FTX crypto valuations rested on speculation rather than underlying value

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02 that FTX crypto assets were sustained primarily by speculative investor sentiment and promises of future appreciation. Michael Lewis, author of the forthcoming book "Going Infinite" about Sam Bankman-Fried, described SBF's ascent as improbable: "Eighteen months earlier, he had nothing. Now he had $22.5 billion." This rapid wealth accumulation—from zero to $22.5 billion in eighteen months—was driven by investor backing and inflated valuations rather than productive assets or cash flows. When market confidence collapsed, the absence of fundamental value underpinning these assets meant the decline was severe and immediate, contributing to what prosecutors characterize as "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."


---


# Defence argues Bankman-Fried acted in good faith, not as villain

Fortune reported on 2023-10-04 that defence lawyer Mark Cohen opened his case by asserting "Sam didn't defraud anyone," positioning the defendant as a "nerdy startup founder who acted in good faith" rather than accepting the prosecution's characterization. Cohen rejected the government's depiction as a "cartoon of a villain," claiming instead that Bankman-Fried's business practices between FTX and Alameda Research were reasonable and that when "the walls came closing in," he demonstrated willingness to use personal wealth to make customers whole, arguing "Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses. He didn't steal any money."


---


# Bankman-Fried's visible distress during Wang's testimony

CNBC reported on 2023-10-06 that Sam Bankman-Fried, founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, remained "mostly quiet in court intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys," but his demeanor shifted markedly as his former MIT classmate and FTX co-founder Gary Wang testified against him. Bankman-Fried "looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground, and at one point putting his head in his hands." Wang testified that he had committed financial crimes including wire and commodities fraud with Bankman-Fried's involvement while both worked at FTX.


---


# Author contests Bankman-Fried's "risk-neutral" framing as gambling addiction

The Verge reported on 2023-10-10 that the author objects to Sam Bankman-Fried's self-characterization during the FTX fraud trial. The author argues that Bankman-Fried's description of himself as "risk-neutral" is misleading language that masks compulsive gambling behavior. This critique extends to Bankman-Fried's reported boast of a 5 percent chance of becoming US president—a claim the author reads through the same lens of reckless risk-taking. The author notes, "Bankman-Fried called this being 'risk-neutral,' which seems like a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict," suggesting the defendant's financial decisions at Alameda Research and FTX reflect pathological betting rather than rational economic strategy.


---


# Bankman-Fried's "focused on solutions" defense undercut by absence of corrective action

The Verge reported on 2023-10-31 that during cross-examination, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon asked Sam Bankman-Fried whether he had investigated who spent the $8 billion that Alameda owed FTX. Bankman-Fried replied, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it" — claiming instead he was "focused on solutions." This objection to an inference of consciousness of wrongdoing is strained because no corrective measures followed the discovery. Sassoon then asked pointedly: "Did he fire anyone? Nope!" No employees were terminated, no repayment protocols established, and no risk management rules implemented to prevent similar misappropriation. The absence of any protective action contradicts the claim of solution-focused intent.


---


# Prosecutors use Bankman-Fried's public statements as evidence of intent in FTX fraud trial

The Verge reported on 2023-09-28 that prosecutors in Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial plan to use his own public communications to establish intent to defraud. The indictment characterizes Bankman-Fried's November 2022 tweets as "false and misleading," according to filings in the case. Prosecutors intend to contrast his public statements on Twitter and in interviews against what actually occurred at FTX, demonstrating that Bankman-Fried knowingly made false claims. His assertions that FTX "segregates customer assets from its own assets" and that "Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX" directly contradicted the reality that Alameda possessed unlimited withdrawal capabilities, prosecutors allege.


---


# SEC characterizes FTX as fraudulent enterprise from inception with multi-billion-dollar customer fund diversion

The Verge reported on 2023-09-28 that the SEC alleges FTX operated as a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." According to prosecutors, founder Sam Bankman-Fried diverted customer deposits to Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. The indictment describes special code features that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, while he publicly claimed Alameda lacked privileged access.


---


# U.S. Attorney characterizes Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes as major financial fraud

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history" at a press conference. Williams made this characterization as Bankman-Fried's criminal trial began, with the former FTX CEO facing seven counts of fraud and conspiracy.

TechCrunch reported on 2023-11-06 that Epic Games filed an antitrust lawsuit against Google, arguing that Google restrains competition in two distinct markets. Epic contends that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior regarding "the distribution of apps to Android users and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps." Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act, California's Cartwright Act, and the Unfair Competition Law. # Gemini announced as Google's flagship generative AI model

Google had stated that Gemini "meets or exceeds the performance of other leading gen AI models like OpenAI's GPT-4," but "anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise."

Independent user reports documented failures across four domains. On factual recall, Gemini Pro gave wrong answers about 2023 Oscar winners—claiming Brendan Gleeson won Best Actor instead of Brendan Fraser. On linguistic constraints, it generated a seven-letter French word when asked for a six-letter one. On news recency, its Ukraine war summary was "over a month out of date." On code generation, users reported that Gemini Pro could not write basic Python functions, HTML analog clocks, or bug-free games on first attempts, whereas ChatGPT succeeded at similar tasks.

TechCrunch reported on 2023-12-07 that Google's promotional materials claimed Gemini "meets or exceeds the performance of other leading gen AI models like OpenAI's GPT-4," yet immediate user reports contradicted this substantially. The tension arises because vendor benchmarks and real-world anecdotes operate in distinct domains. Users documented Gemini Pro failing factual recall (naming wrong Oscar winners), producing confabulations (falsely claiming author Charlie Stross contributed to Linux), struggling with multilingual tasks (providing seven-letter instead of six-letter French words), and underperforming on coding tasks that ChatGPT completed on first attempt.

These failures don't necessarily invalidate Google's architecture or benchmark metrics—which may measure different capabilities under controlled conditions—but they illustrate why anecdotal evidence of concrete task failures can coexist with parity claims. Benchmark performance and deployed usability remain only weakly correlated, allowing both narratives to hold simultaneously without logical contradiction.
